quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Deal with' means 'handle' — the two words move as one unit before the object.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'need to' + phrasal verb (deal with) + object (this issue) + time (today). 'Deal with' means to handle or address a problem.
quests.textToSpeak: I need to deal with this issue today.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Looking forward to' is a three-word chunk expressing excitement about something coming up.
quests.explanation: 'We're' + phrasal verb (looking forward to) + object (the weekend). 'Look forward to' is followed by a noun or '-ing' form, never a plain 'to' infinitive.
quests.textToSpeak: We're looking forward to the weekend.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Gets along with' describes a relationship — it needs all three words together to make sense.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + phrasal verb (gets along with) + object (everyone) + place (at work). 'Get along with' means to have a friendly relationship with someone.
quests.textToSpeak: He gets along with everyone at work.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Caught up on' means 'did enough of something missed before' — all three words stay linked.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + adverb (finally) + phrasal verb (caught up on) + object (my sleep). 'Catch up on' means to do enough of something you fell behind on.
quests.textToSpeak: I finally caught up on my sleep.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Cut down on' means to reduce something gradually, not stop it completely.
quests.explanation: 'She's' + 'trying to' + phrasal verb (cut down on) + object (sugar). 'Cut down on' expresses a gradual reduction rather than a full stop.
quests.textToSpeak: She's trying to cut down on sugar.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Ran out of' means the supply disappeared completely — listen for all three words together.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + phrasal verb (ran out of) + object (milk) + time (this morning). 'Run out of' means to have none left of something.
quests.textToSpeak: We ran out of milk this morning.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: Inside an embedded question, the word order stays like a statement — no inversion happens.
quests.explanation: 'I don't know' + 'why' + subject (the printer) + verb (stopped working). Embedded questions keep normal subject-verb order, unlike direct questions.
quests.textToSpeak: I don't know why the printer stopped working.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'If' introduces the embedded yes/no question, and the word order after it stays normal.
quests.explanation: 'Do you know' + 'if' + subject (the store) + verb (is) + adjective (open) + time (today)? 'If' can introduce an embedded yes/no question.
quests.textToSpeak: Do you know if the store is open today?

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Notice 'is' moves to the very end — different from how a direct question would sound.
quests.explanation: 'Can you tell me' + 'where' + subject (the nearest exit) + verb (is)? In embedded questions, the verb doesn't jump ahead of the subject.
quests.textToSpeak: Can you tell me where the nearest exit is?

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The reporting verb comes first, then the embedded question follows in statement order.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (asked) + object (me) + 'what time' + subject (the train) + verb (left). Reported embedded questions drop the question-word inversion entirely.
quests.textToSpeak: She asked me what time the train left.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'How' introduces the embedded clause, kept in normal statement word order.
quests.explanation: 'I'm not sure' + 'how' + subject (this machine) + verb (works). Uncertainty phrases like 'I'm not sure' often lead into an embedded question.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm not sure how this machine works.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The reason clause follows 'why' in plain statement order, just like the other embedded patterns.
quests.explanation: Subject (Nobody) + verb (explained) + 'why' + subject (the flight) + verb (was delayed). Even negative subjects like 'nobody' can introduce an embedded question.
quests.textToSpeak: Nobody explained why the flight was delayed.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Would' replaces 'will' when reporting what someone said earlier.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (said) + 'that' + reported clause (he would call back later). Reported speech often shifts 'will' back to 'would'.
quests.textToSpeak: He said that he would call back later.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Told' needs an object (me) right after it, unlike 'said' which doesn't.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (told) + object (me) + 'that' + reported clause (the meeting was cancelled). 'Tell' always needs a listener named directly after it.
quests.textToSpeak: She told me that the meeting was cancelled.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Might' softens the reported prediction, showing it isn't certain.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + verb (mentioned) + 'that' + reported clause (prices might increase soon). 'Mentioned' introduces information shared casually, not as a strong claim.
quests.textToSpeak: They mentioned that prices might increase soon.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The 'if' clause uses present tense, even though it describes a future possibility.
quests.explanation: 'If' + condition (it rains, present) + result ('we'll cancel the picnic', will + base). First conditional pairs a present-tense condition with a 'will' result.
quests.textToSpeak: If it rains, we'll cancel the picnic.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: This time the result comes first, and the 'if' condition follows after it.
quests.explanation: Result ('she'll be upset', will + base) + 'if' + condition (you forget her birthday, present). The 'if' clause can follow the result instead of leading the sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: She'll be upset if you forget her birthday.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Both halves talk about the near future, but only one uses 'will'.
quests.explanation: 'If' + condition (you leave now, present) + result ('you'll miss the rush', will + base). The present tense in the 'if' clause still refers to a future situation.
quests.textToSpeak: If you leave now, you'll miss the rush.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Unless' means 'if not' — it sets up a condition by ruling something out.
quests.explanation: 'Unless' + condition (something changes) + result (the deadline stays the same). 'Unless' works like 'if not', introducing an exception.
quests.textToSpeak: Unless something changes, the deadline stays the same.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'As soon as' introduces a time condition, similar in structure to 'if', but about timing.
quests.explanation: 'I'll' + verb (text) + object (you) + 'as soon as' + condition (I land, present). 'As soon as' means 'immediately after', linking two future events.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll text you as soon as I land.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The negative result depends on the missing condition introduced by 'unless'.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'won't' + verb (start) + 'unless' + condition (everyone is ready). 'Unless everyone is ready' means 'only if everyone is ready' in reverse.
quests.textToSpeak: We won't start unless everyone is ready.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The whole subject is one long chunk: adjective, noun, then a phrase describing him further.
quests.explanation: Subject (The tall man in the gray coat) + verb (waved) + 'at us'. A long noun phrase can carry an adjective and a describing phrase before the verb appears.
quests.textToSpeak: The tall man in the gray coat waved at us.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: Two adjectives stack before the noun: personality first, then age.
quests.explanation: Subject (A quiet young woman) + verb (sat) + place (near the window). Multiple adjectives before a noun often follow an opinion-then-age order.
quests.textToSpeak: A quiet young woman sat near the window.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Two adjectives describe the bridge, and the sentence ends with both an adverb and a time phrase.
quests.explanation: Subject (The old wooden bridge) + adverb (finally) + verb (collapsed) + time (last night). Age and material adjectives commonly appear together before a noun.
quests.textToSpeak: The old wooden bridge finally collapsed last night.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Actually' softly signals a slight correction or a new point of view.
quests.explanation: 'Actually' + clause (I think we should wait a bit longer). 'Actually' often introduces a mild contrast with what was expected or said before.
quests.textToSpeak: Actually, I think we should wait a bit longer.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'By the way' introduces a new, less urgent topic in the middle of a conversation.
quests.explanation: 'By the way' + question (did you get my message)? This phrase shifts the conversation to a related but separate topic.
quests.textToSpeak: By the way, did you get my message?

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Honestly' signals that a frank, possibly unwelcome opinion is coming next.
quests.explanation: 'Honestly' + clause (the food wasn't as good as expected). 'Honestly' prepares the listener for a direct, sincere opinion.
quests.textToSpeak: Honestly, the food wasn't as good as expected.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: A conditional and an embedded question combine before the main offer.
quests.explanation: 'If' + condition (you don't know how to fix it, containing an embedded question) + result (I can deal with it myself). A conditional clause can itself contain an embedded question.
quests.textToSpeak: If you don't know how to fix it, I can deal with it myself.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: A reported question and a phrasal verb sit side by side in one natural sentence.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (asked) + 'if' + reported clause (we could catch up sometime next week). Reported questions with 'if' still keep normal statement word order.
quests.textToSpeak: She asked if we could catch up sometime next week.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Three skills combine: a discourse marker, an embedded question, and a contrast connector.
quests.explanation: 'Honestly' + 'I'm not sure' + embedded question (why he didn't show up) + 'but' + result (I'll ask him later). Natural spoken English often stacks several small structures into one flowing sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Honestly, I'm not sure why he didn't show up, but I'll ask him later.
